A1-A2.headline: The Ancient Computer from the Sea

pages.text: Around 1900, divers found a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera. They brought many old things out of the water in 1900 and 1901. One item was a box with metal gears inside. Scientists call this the Antikythera mechanism. It is the oldest known machine of its kind, built long ago in the second century BC.
pages.caption: A hypothetical reconstruction of the mechanism of Antikythera at the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology, in Athens, Greece.

evidence.articleCaption: A hypothetical reconstruction of the mechanism of Antikythera at the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology, in Athens, Greece.

pages.text: The machine was very complex for its time. It used many bronze gears to work. People think it was used to track the Sun and the Moon. People still debate whether it could show where planets were in the sky. It helped people know when eclipses would happen many years in advance.

The device had a wooden case. It had doors with writing on them. This writing acted like an instruction manual. It told people how to use the machine. It even tracked the four-year cycle of famous athletic games, which were like the ancient Olympic Games.

Scientists used X-rays to look inside the broken pieces. They found at least 30 gears. This level of skill was not seen again in Europe until the 14th century. It shows that ancient people were very good at math and science, even without modern tools or electricity.

We do not know exactly who built it. It might have been based on ideas from famous astronomers. Today, all the pieces are kept in a museum in Athens. They help us understand how people in the past studied the stars and the world around them.

B1-B2.headline: Unlocking the Secrets of the Antikythera Mechanism

pages.text: Around 1900, sponge divers discovered a shipwreck off the coast of Antikythera, Greece. Among the retrieved treasures was a corroded lump of bronze and wood. This artifact, now known as the Antikythera mechanism, is recognized as the earliest known analogue computer, often dated to the second century BC.
pages.caption: A hypothetical reconstruction of the mechanism of Antikythera at the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology, in Athens, Greece.

evidence.articleCaption: A hypothetical reconstruction of the mechanism of Antikythera at the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology, in Athens, Greece.

pages.text: The device was housed in a wooden case and contained at least 30 meshing bronze gears. Through high-resolution X-ray tomography, researchers revealed that the mechanism functioned as an orrery. It modeled the movements of the Sun and Moon, predicted eclipses, and tracked the irregular orbit of the Moon.

Beyond astronomy, the mechanism served as a calendar. It tracked the Metonic and Callippic cycles and even monitored the timing of panhellenic games, such as the ancient Olympic Games. Inscriptions on the device served as an instruction manual, detailing how to operate the complex system of dials and gears.

The craftsmanship suggests a high level of Hellenistic scientific expertise. Similar mechanical complexity did not reappear in Europe until the 14th century. While the exact date of construction remains debated, evidence points to the late second or early first century BC, relying on advanced mathematical theories of the time.

Today, the 82 fragments of the mechanism are preserved at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. While some parts are likely missing, the device remains a testament to ancient engineering. It highlights a sophisticated tradition of astronomical modeling that was rarely preserved due to the value of bronze.

C1-C2.headline: The Antikythera Mechanism: An Ancient Engineering Feat

pages.text: Retrieved from a shipwreck off Antikythera in 1901, the Antikythera mechanism represents a pinnacle of Hellenistic engineering. Often dated to the second century BC, this artifact is classified as the earliest known analogue computer. Its discovery provided unprecedented insight into the sophisticated mechanical capabilities of ancient Greek scientists and astronomers.
pages.caption: A hypothetical reconstruction of the mechanism of Antikythera at the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology, in Athens, Greece.

pages.text: The device, originally encased in a wooden frame, utilized a complex gear train of at least 30 bronze components. Advanced imaging techniques have allowed researchers to map these gears, which modeled celestial mechanics, including the Moon's perigee and apogee, and predicted solar and lunar eclipses with remarkable precision for the era.

The mechanism's functionality extended to chronometry and social administration. It integrated the Sothic Egyptian calendar with the zodiacal ecliptic and tracked the four-year cycles of panhellenic athletic festivals. Deciphered inscriptions on the casing fragments serve as a technical manual, confirming the device's role in tracking multi-year astronomical and cultural cycles.

The precision of the gearing implies the existence of a broader tradition of mechanical design, likely lost as bronze artifacts were frequently recycled. Modern simulations of possible planetary displays reveal limits in Greek theories of planetary motion; they do not prove exactly how the ancient device handled every planet. The surviving gears nevertheless show rare craftsmanship, while related bronze artifacts often disappeared through recycling.

Current research continues to analyze the 82 identified fragments housed in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. By synthesizing epigraphic evidence with mechanical reconstruction, scholars have moved closer to understanding the device's original calibration and its place within the broader context of ancient Mediterranean scientific and mathematical thought.
